summary: Sets out requirements for a framework and protocols to access and update Internet Media Guide information for media-on-demand and multicast applications. They are meant to guide the choice and development of efficient, scalable protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist of what a good TV-guide system for the Internet must be able to do before anyone builds it.

subtitle: Building scalable systems to guide users through media content and services.

tldr.problem: As media services spread across the Internet—TV channels, radio, video-on-demand, live events—there is no standard way to deliver metadata about what content is available and how to access it. Existing protocols like SAP and HTTP have limitations in scalability, update notification, and flexibility.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4473 sets out requirements for a framework and transport protocols that can deliver Internet Media Guide (IMG) metadata efficiently to large audiences. The requirements cover scalability, consistency management, customization, security, and support for diverse network conditions including wireless and intermittent connections.
tldr.outcome: These requirements guide the design of future IMG protocols and delivery mechanisms, ensuring systems can handle large-scale metadata distribution with timely updates and proper access control.

today: RFC 4473 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It set requirements that guided the development of IMG-related protocols, including frameworks specified in companion documents like RFC 4435.

sections.title: The Problem with Media Guides
sections.content:
For decades, the Internet has used simple protocols like Session Announcement Protocol (SAP) to broadcast information about multimedia sessions and the Session Description Protocol (SDP) to describe them. These work well for small audiences but break down when serving millions of users across diverse networks.

As the Internet grows to support not just conferences but also broadcast TV, radio, live events, video-on-demand, distance learning, and gaming, there is a need for a flexible framework to describe and deliver metadata about all these services. Current protocols either limit metadata size, require multicast infrastructure, or rely on polling that doesn't scale.
sections.plainLanguage: Old systems worked fine for small groups. Now we need something that can send the same program guide to millions of people, over phone lines, wireless networks, and broadband, and tell them when shows change.

sections.title: What Is an Internet Media Guide
sections.content:
An Internet Media Guide (IMG) is a structured collection of metadata describing multimedia services—television programs, radio schedules, video streams, downloadable files, or conference sessions. It is a generalization of the Electronic Program Guide (EPG) found on digital TV receivers.

An IMG consists of IMG metadata (the actual content describing services), an IMG sender (the entity publishing the guide), and one or more IMG receivers (users or their devices consuming it). The framework must support one sender and many receivers, but also transitive sharing where receivers become senders to pass metadata forward.

An IMG delivery system moves this metadata from senders to receivers. It handles both push delivery (sender initiates) and pull delivery (receiver requests), and must notify receivers when metadata changes.
sections.plainLanguage: An IMG is like a TV guide. It says what shows are available, when they play, what you need to watch them, and how to find them. The system that delivers guides to millions of TVs is what these requirements describe.

sections.title: Key Requirements for IMG Systems
sections.content:
RFC 4473 groups requirements into five main areas:

General Requirements: The system MUST support any metadata format and allow receivers to get information from multiple senders at once. It MUST be modular, allowing the combination of several transport operations.

Delivery Properties: The system MUST scale to enormous numbers of receivers and metadata items. It MUST handle intermittent connectivity (critical for mobile users), implement Internet-friendly congestion control, and offer both sender-driven (broadcast-style) and receiver-driven (on-demand) delivery.

Customization: IMG receivers often want only a subset of available metadata based on their preferences. The system MUST support this filtering without breaking scalability.

Reliability and Consistency: IMG metadata changes over time as programs are added, removed, or rescheduled. The system MUST manage consistency between senders and receivers, either through synchronization or by notifying receivers of changes. Receivers MUST be able to get reliable message delivery.

Description and Security: Metadata MUST be structured for efficient delivery in fragments. The system MUST support metadata authentication, integrity checking, access control, and protection against denial-of-service and replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A good IMG system must work for billions of pieces of information, handle network failures, let you pick just what you want to watch, keep everyone's information up to date, and make sure the guide you receive really comes from the broadcaster and hasn't been faked.

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates IMG requirements through diverse use cases spanning different network types and applications:

IP Datacast to wireless receivers: Mobile devices with limited batteries receive metadata over unidirectional broadcast. The system must support carouselled (repeated) delivery, forward error correction, and the ability to wake up periodically to receive updates without draining the battery.

Dial-up connections: Users on slow links need locally cached metadata and prefer avoiding large downloads, suggesting support for incremental updates rather than retransmitting entire guides.

Media services: TV and radio programs can be scheduled, rescheduled (affecting later programs), and described with detailed metadata for user selection. Live event coverage may include unexpected schedule changes and auxiliary information delivered over multiple networks.

Specialized content: Distance learning, multiplayer gaming, file distribution, and advance notice of coming releases all require metadata that varies in structure and temporal properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must work on your phone in a subway, your old computer on dial-up, a TV in your living room, and a gaming console at a friend's house. Programs get rescheduled, shows have warnings, and everyone's situation is different.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
IMG systems distribute information across networks and intermediaries, raising several security concerns:

Authentication and integrity: It MUST be possible to authenticate the originator of IMG metadata and subparts of it, and to validate integrity even after individual pieces are separated and recombined.

Privacy: Customized metadata and notification to individuals can reveal viewing habits. The system MUST support confidential user requests and metadata delivery, ideally end-to-end to prevent intermediaries from seeing sensitive information.

Access control: Some metadata may be freely available while other parts require authorization. Different parts of the same guide may need different protection levels. Users MUST be able to access some metadata anonymously and avoid being identified.

Denial-of-service protection: IMG operations SHOULD be authenticated, and the system SHOULD prevent attackers from exhausting sender resources by creating many sessions or flooding metadata.

Replay protection: Since IMG metadata is updated or invalidated over time, the system MUST prevent attackers from replacing current metadata with older versions, and MUST protect against replay attacks on IMG operations themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to trust that the guide really came from the TV company, not from someone pretending to be them. People's viewing habits should be private. Some channels should require you to log in, others should work without saying who you are. The system shouldn't let hackers send fake guides or overwhelm servers with billions of fake requests.
